units.summary: Marimar and Mar Zutra would demolish and rebuild their seasonal homes during the opposite seasons to ensure they always had a place to stay.
Rav Ashi noticed cracks in the synagogue of Mata Mehasya, demolished it, and moved his bed into the site to ensure he would not leave until the new structure was completed.

Herod, a slave of the Hasmoneans, rebels and kills his masters to take the throne, leading to the suicide of the last Hasmonean princess and Herod's subsequent massacre of the Sages. Herod, after blinding Bava ben Buta and killing the Sages, tests the surviving rabbi in disguise, eventually repents, and follows the rabbi's advice to rebuild the Temple as atonement.
Ravina builds walls around Ronya's field and, after Ronya refuses to pay, tricks him into revealing his appreciation for the walls during a date harvest, leading Rava to rule that Ronya must pay.
When Ronya buys land next to Ravina, Ravina considers evicting him, but Rav Safra convinces him to let the poor man stay.
The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa, Rav Huna, and Mar bar Rav Ashi ruled in actual cases according to different sides of the debate between Reish Lakish and Abaye/Rava.
A resident of a sinking lower story asks his upstairs neighbor to help rebuild, but the neighbor refuses because his own living space remains functional.
A man blocks his neighbor's windows with a wall and offers various structural compromises, all of which the neighbor rejects due to concerns about the house's stability.
Two brothers divide their father's estate, and the one who received the garden builds a wall that blocks the light of the one who received the hall.
A case involving orphans with a promissory note and a borrower with a receipt is brought before Rav Hama, who rules that the debt cannot be collected but the note should not be destroyed.
A pious man who regularly spoke with Elijah built a gatehouse, causing Elijah to stop appearing to him because the gatehouse prevented the poor from being heard.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia taxes the Sages for a wall, leading Reish Lakish to protest and later consult Rabbi Yoḥanan about the scriptural basis for exempting scholars.
During a famine, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refuses to feed the ignorant, but his disciple Yonatan ben Amram receives food by pretending to be ignorant, leading to a realization by the Rabbi.
When a heavy tax is imposed on Tiberias, the residents flee in groups after Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refuses to make the Sages contribute, eventually leaving the city empty.

Passage B is a distinct incident involving Rabba and the orphans of bar Maryon, featuring a specific action, a challenge by Abaye, and a resolution, which is then followed by the separate incident in Passage A involving Ifera Hurmiz.
The mother of King Shapur sends money to Rav Yosef for a 'great mitzva,' prompting him to determine what that mitzva is.
Rabbi (Judah HaNasi) once appointed two brothers to be in charge of the charity fund.
Rava forced Rav Natan bar Ami to contribute four hundred zuz to charity.
Rabba initially refused to sit on synagogue mats bought with charity funds until he learned that the townspeople have the right to change the designation of such funds.
Two butchers make a scheduling agreement, one violates it, the other destroys his hide in retaliation, and Rava subsequently fines the destroyer.
A poor person approaches Rav Pappa for charity and is ignored, leading Rav Sama to rebuke Rav Pappa for his inaction.
Rava begins to quote a teaching from Ulla.
After Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami mocks Rav Sheshet during a legal debate, he is supernaturally punished with muteness and the loss of his Torah knowledge, leading his mother to plead for his restoration.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai uses a dream prediction to trick his nephews into giving charity so that the money they were destined to lose would go to a mitzva rather than the government.
Rav Pappa nearly falls from a ladder and concludes that this near-accident was a divine punishment for failing to properly assist a poor person.
Yosef the son of Rabbi Yehoshua has a near-death experience, returns to life, and describes the inverted social hierarchy of the next world to his father.
The mother of King Shapur sends a large donation to the rabbis; Rabbi Ami refuses it, but Rava accepts it to maintain peace with the government, leading to a conflict between the two sages.
A queen mother sends money to Rabbi Ami who refuses it, but Rava accepts it for political peace, leading to a conflict between the two rabbis.
During a drought, Binyamin the Righteous finds the charity fund empty and uses his own money to save a starving woman and her children.
Mar bar Rav Ashi hears an imbecile's prophecy and strategically detains rabbinic messengers to ensure his own appointment over Rav Aḥa of Difti.
The young daughter of Rav Ḥisda prophetically declares she wants to marry both Rava and Rami bar Ḥama, which eventually comes to pass.
A man who bought land adjacent to his father's estate requests that specific plot upon his father's death, leading to a dispute with his brothers and a ruling by Rav Yosef.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where Baitos ben Zunin owned a combined scroll of eight Prophets with the approval of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Rav Huna and Rav Aha bar Ya'akov attempt to write Torah scrolls with perfectly matching dimensions, and when Rav Aha succeeds, the Sages cast an 'evil eye' upon him.
The Sages tell Rav Hamnuna that Rabbi Ami wrote four hundred Torah scrolls, and Rav Hamnuna skeptically suggests he only wrote a single verse four hundred times.
A sage sitting before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani claims that Job was merely a parable and never actually existed, prompting a rebuttal from the Rabbi.
A baraita describes a pious gentile named Job who, upon being afflicted by God, blasphemed, leading God to pay his full reward in this world to exclude him from the afterlife.
The Gemara recounts and expands upon the biblical narrative of Job, including the Satan's challenges to God, the destruction of Job's property, and the subsequent dialogue between Job and the Divine.
When a daughter was born to Rabbi Shimon, he was upset, leading his father and Bar Kappara to offer differing perspectives on the blessing of female children.
While Ravina and Rav Hama debated the repentance of Ishmael, Rava dozed off, only to wake up and provide the definitive answer.
The Gemara recounts the historical evolution of the Jewish school system, culminating in Yehoshua ben Gamla's decree to establish local schools to prevent the loss of Torah knowledge.

Joab returns from a six-month campaign in Edom to report to King David regarding the killing of the males. Joab justifies his incomplete genocide of Edom to King David by blaming his teacher's misreading of a verse, leading Joab to confront and nearly kill the teacher.
It contains a specific incident where Rava grants a legal exemption to Rabbi Yoshiya and Rav Ovadya, though it is embedded within a larger legal discussion.
Basket sellers bring goods to Babylonia, are blocked by locals, and Ravina rules on their right to sell to other outsiders.
Wool sellers in Pum Nahara are blocked by locals and Rav Kahana rules on the conditions under which they may sell.
Rav Dimi's figs rot after Rav Adda bar Abba fails him on a scholarly test, leading to a series of curses and the eventual death of Rav Adda.

Rav Yosef attempts to evict bloodletters whose work attracts crows that damage his palm trees. Rav Yosef attempts to evict bloodletters from under his palm trees because the blood they shed attracts crows that damage his dates, leading to a legal dispute with Abaye.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks a pedantic question about a chick's legs and is subsequently expelled from the study hall.
Ravina permits a barrel of wine found in a vineyard of forbidden orla grapes, reasoning that thieves would not hide stolen goods in the same place they stole them.
Rava permits wine found in jugs between vines, assuming it does not belong to a gentile.
Rav Sheshet, who was blind, instructs his servant to position him for prayer in any direction except east, explaining his reasoning.
Pappei Yona’a, having become wealthy and built a mansion, brings a complaint to Rav Ashi because his neighbors' sesame-pressing work causes his house to shake.
The household of bar Maryon caused harm to neighbors while beating flax, leading the neighbors to bring the case before Ravina.
Rav Yosef demands that Rava bar Rav Hanan cut down palm trees that attract crop-destroying birds, but Rava refuses to do so himself, fearing the divine retribution that befell Rabbi Hanina's son.
Rav Pappa discovers Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua digging up and cutting the roots of Rav Pappa's trees that had spread into his field.

Rami bar Ḥama and Rav Ukva bar Ḥama purchase a maidservant and alternate her years of service, but Rava rules that this pattern prevents them from establishing legal presumption of ownership against outsiders.
A man claims a house held by another, arguing he was in a distant marketplace and unaware of the occupation, leading Rav Nachman to demand proof of usage from the possessor.
A man sells all his 'bar Sisin' property but later claims a specific parcel known by that name was not included in the sale.
A property owner challenges a possessor, who claims he bought it, but the owner argues he was away in the outer markets and thus could not protest.

A man challenges a land possessor who claims to have bought the field from a third party who supposedly bought it from the original owner. A claimant successfully argues that a possessor has no standing because the possessor admits the land wasn't bought from the claimant, leading Rava to rule in the claimant's favor.
A possessor argues the claimant once encouraged him to buy the land, but the claimant explains he only did so because the new owner would be easier to litigate against, a claim Rava accepts.
Passage B is a distinct legal case with its own set of arguments and a specific ruling by Rava, following the same formulaic opening as Passage A but involving a different legal defense.
Two people dispute land ownership with conflicting claims of ancestral rights, leading one litigant to change his plea after legal intervention.
Two people claim ancestral land and both bring witnesses of usage, leading Rav Nahman to rule that the land returns to the proven ancestral line.
Following a dispute over land where new evidence is brought, Rav Nahman reverses his initial ruling and physically enforces the transfer of property despite legal objections from Rava.

A man challenges another's right to land, and the possessor claims he bought it and produces a bill of sale. A man claiming land ownership whispers to Rabba that his deed is forged but his claim is true, leading to a legal debate between Rabba and Rav Yosef.
In a debt dispute, the creditor whispers to Rava that his promissory note is forged but the debt is valid, mirroring the previous land case.
A guarantor and debtor dispute whether a repaid debt was subsequently re-borrowed, leading Rav Idi bar Avin to seek a ruling from Abaye.
Abaye confronts Rava bar Sharshom regarding a rumor that he is illegally consuming the produce of orphans' land.

Rav Idi bar Avin and a relative dispute an inheritance; after the relative admits Rav Idi is the rightful heir, a new conflict arises over the produce consumed in the interim. A relative of Rav Idi bar Avin admits he is not the closest heir after seizing a tree, leading to a ruling on the produce he consumed.
It introduces a new legal dispute with different claims and evidence, though the narrative outcome and the rabbi's ruling follow in the subsequent text.
A man claims to have bought land but can only prove two years of possession, leading Rav Nachman to order the return of the land and its produce.
A man claims to have purchased land and brings a single witness to three years of possession, sparking a debate about the validity of a single witness in such cases.
A man snatches metal from another and, when confronted in court with a witness, admits to the act but claims the metal was his, leading to a famous ruling by Rabbi Abba.
Two people dispute ownership of a boat, leading one to have the court seize it while he searches for witnesses, only to return empty-handed and request its release.
In Neharde’a, a man whose barley was eaten by goats seized the animals and claimed damages, leading Shmuel’s father to rule that he could claim up to the value of the goats.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina asks the students of Rabbi Yohanan for their teacher's ruling regarding the number of witnesses required for a protest.
Giddel bar Minyumi lodged a property protest before three rabbis and returned a year later to do so again, only to be told that his first protest remained valid.
A man who mortgaged his orchard is threatened by the creditor that unless he sells the land, the creditor will hide the mortgage and claim ownership through three years of possession.
A man wishing to marry a woman who demanded all his property secretly gifted it to his son first so that his subsequent gift to her would be legally void.

After a flood destroyed his boundary wall, Rav Anan rebuilt it on his neighbor's land with the neighbor's help, but Rav Nahman ruled the land must be returned because the neighbor's consent was based on a mistake.

Rav Kahana's boundary wall was swept away by a flood, and he inadvertently rebuilt it on land that did not belong to him. Rav Kahana is sued by a neighbor for encroaching on land, and after Rav Yehuda rules against him based on contradictory witnesses, Kahana challenges the legal basis and promises to bring a letter from Eretz Yisrael to prove the ruling wrong.
A man living in a loft is challenged by the owner, leading to a discussion where Rav observes Rabbi Hiyya's reaction to the possibility of a quick, undocumented sale.
Rava or Rav Pappa issues a public announcement regarding the legal liability of a seller when a gentile seizes the sold donkey from the buyer.
Abaye shows Rava how the swindlers of Pumbedita manipulate legal claims by first denying they received an item and then claiming they bought it once witnesses prove they have it.
Tavi physically suspended Pafi from a tree to force him to sell a field, leading Rabba bar bar Ḥana to sign both the bill of sale and a secret declaration nullifying it.
Rav Ḥisda rules in a case according to Rabbi Elazar, prompting the grandsons of Rav to confront him for ignoring their grandfather's authority.
As the wife of Rabba bar bar Hana is dying, she declares that certain rings belong to others, leading her husband to seek Rav's guidance on whether to follow her word.
Rava removed a pair of scissors and a book from orphans' possession after a claimant identified them as his own.
A woman used a palm tree for thirteen years, but when a man performed a valid act of plowing, the court awarded him the property because her actions did not constitute legal acquisition.
Rav acquired a garden for his academy by drawing an image on its wall, demonstrating his legal ruling on acquisition.
Rav Huna purchased land from a gentile, but another Jew performed an act of possession first, leading Rav Nachman to rule against Rav Huna.
When a witness on a document died, his brother and another person came to ratify the signature, leading Ravina and Rav Ashi to debate if such testimony is valid.
Rabbi Bena’a visits the Cave of Machpelah, interacts with Eliezer to view Abraham and Sarah, and is eventually warned by a Divine Voice when approaching Adam's burial place.
A magus desecrating graves is physically seized by the deceased Rav Tovi bar Mattana until Abaye intervenes to free him.
Rabbi Bena’a solves a riddle-based inheritance left by a father to his sons using symbolic interpretation.

After Rabbi Bena’a's wife confuses the authorities with a riddle, Bena’a is summoned to explain it, leading to his appointment as a judge. Rabbi Bena'a continues his journey, correcting flawed or simplistic maxims inscribed on city gates, leading the locals to rewrite their laws based on his wisdom.
Rabbi Oshaya disagrees with his father Rabbi Hama on a ruling and consults his grandfather Rabbi Bisa, leading Rami bar Hama to praise the three generations of scholars.
A man brought a case to Rabbi Ammi, who sent him to Rabbi Abba bar Memel.
A man who opened windows into a shared courtyard sought legal validation from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and subsequently from Rabbi Ḥiyya.
A man being forced to remove a projection into the public domain challenges Rabbi Ami for having his own projection, leading to a distinction between public domains and private alleyways.

A man whose tree is being protested by the public comes to Rabbi Yannai for a ruling, while Rabbi Yannai himself owns a similar tree. Rabbi Yannai secretly cuts down his own leaning tree at night so that he can ethically and legally command another man to do the same the following day.

Following the destruction of the Second Temple, Rabbi Yehoshua uses a series of logical arguments to convince a group of extreme ascetics to adopt a more moderate and sustainable form of national mourning.
A man offered to sell land called 'the house of Hiyya,' and Rav Ashi ruled that since there were two such plots, the seller only intended to sell one.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi challenge Rav's ruling on the boundaries of a sold field, and Rav remains silent.
Abaye challenges Rabba's ruling and assumes Rabba's silence means agreement, only to later discover deeds from Rabba's house that prove Rabba held his original position.
A man sold an olive press 'and its accompaniments,' leading to a dispute over external stores that was brought before Rav Yosef for a ruling.

A man instructs that a house containing 100 barrels be given as a gift, but when it is found to contain 120, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi debate whether the recipient receives the whole house or only the specified capacity.
Rabba recounts a report from seafarers about how they use clubs inscribed with divine names to strike down dangerous waves topped with white fire.
Seafarers recount a time they were lifted so high by a wave they saw a star's resting place and overheard waves discussing the divine decree that prevents them from flooding the world.

Rabba describes seeing the demon Hurmin outrunning a horseman on the walls of Mehoza and begins to describe a second incident involving mules. Hurmin bar Lilith performs an incredible feat of agility and coordination by jumping between bridges and pouring wine between cups during a storm without spilling.
Rabba describes seeing a massive day-old antelope whose waste was so large it dammed the Jordan river.
Rabba bar bar Hana witnesses a giant frog being swallowed by a snake, which is then swallowed by a raven that flies into a massive tree.
Rabba bar bar Hana recounts seeing a giant fish killed by an insect, which washed ashore, destroyed districts, and then provided food and building materials for the survivors.
Travelers mistake a giant fish for an island, but when they light a fire to cook, the fish feels the heat and flips over, nearly drowning them.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes a ship journey that took three days just to pass between two fins of a single giant fish.
Travelers see a bird standing in water and think it is shallow, but a Divine Voice warns them that a carpenter's axe has been falling in that spot for seven years without hitting bottom.
Rabba bar bar Hana encounters incredibly fat geese in the desert and receives a physical sign from them regarding his portion in the World-to-Come.

An Arab guide uses his desert skills to lead Rabba bar bar Hana to see the preserved bodies of the Israelites who died in the wilderness after the Exodus. Rabba bar bar Hana visits the 'dead of the wilderness', cuts a piece of their clothing to determine the law of ritual fringes, and is rebuked by the Sages for his foolishness.
Rabba bar bar Hana is shown Mount Sinai and hears God lamenting an oath, but is later rebuked by the Sages for not nullifying the oath on the spot.
The Arab shows Rabba bar bar Hana the site where Korah was swallowed, using wet wool on a spear to demonstrate the heat rising from the earth.
Rabba bar bar Hana leaves his basket at the junction of heaven and earth while praying, only to find it has moved away due to the rotation of the heavenly sphere.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rav Safra describe sightings of fantastic sea creatures while traveling by ship.

Rabbi Yohanan sees a treasure crate in the sea and a diver attempts to retrieve it. A diver attempts to retrieve a chest from the sea but is attacked by a fish, which he repels with vinegar before a Divine Voice identifies the chest as belonging to Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's wife.
Rav Yehuda relates a sea voyage where a diver's attempt to take a gem led to a snake attack, a raven's intervention, and a miraculous revival of the snake by another of its kind.
While at sea, Rabbi Yehoshua is startled by a great light, waking Rabbi Eliezer, who explains that they have seen the eyes of the leviathan.
Huna bar Natan recounts how a thigh of meat they had prepared in the desert miraculously healed itself after being placed on a certain type of grass.
During creation, the Minister of the Sea refused God's command to shrink the waters, resulting in God striking him dead.
A student mocks Rabbi Yoḥanan's teaching about giant precious stones in the future, but after seeing angels preparing them at sea, he returns to apologize and is rebuked.
Rabbi Yosei recalls seeing the city of Tzippori in its prime with its numerous markets.
Rav Pappa successfully retrieves twelve thousand dinars from Bei Ḥozai by legally transferring ownership to Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa via his house's threshold.

Rabbi Yehuda recounts an incident in Tzalmon where a man planted vines at specific intervals and manipulated the branches to allow for sowing other crops between the rows. Rav Yosef recounts an incident in the village of shepherds where Rav Yehuda ordered a seller of trees to provide the buyer with enough land for an ox and its equipment.
Upon arriving in Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Elazar asks Ze'eiri to identify the scholar who holds Rav's traditions on measures, and Ze'eiri points out Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi.
A man examining meat in a butcher shop has it stolen by a horseman, and Rav Yeimar rules that the man is liable for the cost because he had already lifted it.
After the House of the Nasi appointed price inspectors, Karna taught a ruling in their favor, leading Shmuel to curse him such that a physical growth appeared in Karna's eye.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel creates a new volume measure and the Sages challenge its legality based on Shmuel's rulings.
The Gemara contrasts the market practices of Shmuel and his father and reports a message from Eretz Yisrael regarding whose merit is greater.
During a drought, Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina instructs his attendant Puga to store produce for the coming years.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya used to profit from selling wine and oil.
The Gemara discusses the deaths of Elimelech's family and the tragedy of Ibzan's children as consequences of their actions.
The Gemara recounts Abraham's imprisonment for his faith and the global mourning upon his death.
A continuation of a lament regarding the death of Abraham, using the metaphor of a ship losing its captain.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar recall specific physical manifestations of the extreme abundance and famine they witnessed in their youth.
Rav Yosef issues rulings in two cases involving spoiled beer and wine based on the opinions of Rav and Shmuel.
Rabbi Ḥanina travels to rural villages to teach and addresses a contradiction between biblical verses regarding the dimensions of the Sanctuary.
When litigants came before Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami regarding a path through a vineyard, he ruled that the path must be wide enough for a person to carry a load of branches and turn around.
When Rav Avya's wife died, he performed the mourning ritual of standing and sitting, but Rav Yosef, Abaye, and Rava ruled that he had erred in several aspects of the performance.

An incident in Sepphoris involving a rental agreement with contradictory terms was brought before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yosei, who ruled that the parties should divide the value of the intercalated month.

Rav Pappa buys a field specified as twenty griv, but upon measuring it and finding only fifteen, he takes the seller to court before Abaye. Rav Pappa buys land that turns out to be smaller than the seller claimed, but when he sues, Abaye rules that he must accept the discrepancy because he was familiar with the field.

Jonathan, a descendant of Moses, justifies his service as an idolatrous priest through a misunderstood family tradition until King David redirects his love for money by appointing him as the Temple treasurer.
Rav Nittai and Rabbi Tabla attempt to rule according to Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav but are sharply rebuked and stopped by Shmuel.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya intends to rule like Rabbi Zekharya but is challenged by Rav Nahman.
The elderly and blind Rabbi Yannai, while walking supported by his attendant Rabbi Simlai, is approached by Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, leading to a physical encounter and a legal inquiry.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai confronts a group of Sadducees regarding inheritance laws and successfully silences an old man who attempts to challenge him with a logical argument.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, having lost ten sons, would carry a bone of his tenth son to console others in their grief.
Rabbi Yosei bar Natan travels from Neharde’a to Meḥoza to find Rav Sheshet and ask for an explanation of a baraita.
Ulla explains that the 15th of Av is significant because King Hoshea removed the guards Jeroboam had placed to prevent pilgrimage.
Rav Mattana explains that the 15th of Av is the day the victims of Beitar were buried, leading to the institution of the 'HaTov VeHaMetiv' blessing.
A baraita lists seven individuals whose overlapping lives spanned the entirety of human history.
The baraita describes the miraculous process by which Elazar the High Priest and Joshua used the Urim VeTummim and a lottery to divide the Land of Israel among the tribes.

Rav Aḥa bar Rav reports to Ravina that Ameimar visited his town and taught a specific ruling regarding a firstborn's inheritance of loans, which Ravina then explains as following the school of Neharde'a.

A dying man leaves his property to his grandmother and then his heirs, leading to a complex inheritance dispute when his daughter and grandmother die in a specific order. A man leaves his property to his grandmother and then to his heirs, leading to a legal dispute when his daughter predeceases the grandmother and her husband claims the estate.
A firstborn sold his deceased brother's portion of an estate, leading the brother's orphans to physically reclaim the produce from the buyers until Rava ruled on the sale's validity.
Mar Zutra, a firstborn, divided a basket of peppers equally with his brothers, and Rav Ashi ruled that this act constituted a waiver of his firstborn rights for the entire estate.
A man testifies before Rabba bar bar Hana that someone is a firstborn because his father called him a 'foolish firstborn', but the Rabbi questions the validity of this proof.
A man proves someone is a firstborn to Rabbi Hanina by testifying that the father used to send people with eye ailments to the son, whose saliva had healing properties unique to a father's firstborn.
After Rav Pappa challenges him with a tradition from Eretz Yisrael, Rava publicly retracts his previous legal ruling, declaring it a mistake.
The residents of Akra De’Agma ask Shmuel a legal question about a father's credibility regarding a firstborn, and Shmuel provides a ruling.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi initially dismisses a challenge from Rabbi Natan regarding a Mishnaic text but later retracts his answer, admitting his previous response was born of immaturity.
Rabbi Yehuda the baker recounts an incident where his son gave all his property to his wife, but the Sages ruled she lost her marriage contract and the gift was nullified by a debt.

A dying man divides his estate between his daughters and wife, leading Rav Nahman to visit Rav Hisda in Sura to determine if the wife's specific portion of produce causes her to lose her marriage contract rights.
A man divides his property among his wife and two daughters, but after one daughter dies, Rav Pappi must determine how the returned portion affects the wife's share.
A dying man is asked who should inherit his property and he responds with a rhetorical question.
Rav Ilish proposes a compromise in a complex inheritance case but is corrected and embarrassed by Rava, who then comforts him with a biblical verse.

After being disinherited by his father Yosef ben Yo’ezer, the son finds a massive pearl and, through clever negotiation, donates a vast sum to the Temple, leading the treasurers to compare his piety to his father's.

Yonatan ben Uzziel receives an inheritance meant to disinherit a man's children, but he redistributes it, leading to a physical confrontation and verbal debate with Shammai. Shammai attempts to protest Yonatan ben Uzziel's distribution of an inheritance but is silenced by Yonatan's logic and admits his mistake.
A man in Beit Horon tries to gift a wedding feast to a friend so his forbidden father can eat, but the friend consecrates the feast to the Temple, sparking a confrontation.
When Yonatan ben Uzziel studied Torah, the intensity of his sanctity was so great that any bird flying over him would be burned.
Rav Yosef, having lost his memory due to illness, realizes a logical flaw in a tradition he cited and corrects himself.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef brings a ruling from Eretz Yisrael that contradicts Rav Yosef, prompting Rav Sheshet to dismissively wave his hand.
A dying man declares his wife fit for a High Priest to exempt her from levirate marriage, leading to a debate between Rava and Abaye and a final ruling to remain concerned about her status.
A man declares on his deathbed that he has no brothers, and despite Rav Yosef's argument for leniency, Rava rules that the court must remain concerned about the wife's status.
Rav Huna and Rav Naḥman visit the ailing Rabba bar Avuh and use the opportunity to clarify a halakhic ruling regarding Rabbi Yosei's opinion.
The Sages test the knowledge of Abaye and Rava's scribes regarding a legal distinction.
A woman gives a palm tree to Rav Beivai bar Abaye for his lifetime to stop him from being angry when she harvests it, but he then transfers it to his son, prompting a sharp rebuke from Rav Huna.
Rabbi Abbahu tells Rabbi Yirmeya to return the next day for an answer to his legal inquiry, and then provides a ruling.
A man tells his wife that his property should go to her fetus, and Rav Huna rules that a fetus cannot acquire property.
The Gemara cites an incident where a fetus moved three times after its mother had already died to challenge a legal assumption about the order of death.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hana to assemble ten men so he can publicly declare that a fetus can acquire property.
An older son confronts his father for promising all property to future children, leading the father to grant him an equal share.
A man declares his property belongs to his wife and sons, and Rav Yosef rules that the wife receives half.
The Gemara cites precedents in Neharde'a and Tiberias where Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan actively intervened to ensure an individual received half of a shared gift.
A man sends silk to his family without instructions, and Rabbi Ami determines the distribution based on which garments are suitable for sons versus daughters.
A man with a son and daughter leaves his property to his 'sons', leading to a linguistic debate on whether the plural includes a single son.
A man leaves property to his 'sons' when he has a son and a grandson, prompting a debate on whether a grandson is legally considered a son.
Rav Safra invested money left by his father into a business, leading his brothers to sue him for a portion of the profits.
A man sent massive amounts of gifts to his father-in-law and drank a small amount there before dying, leading the Sages of Usha to determine which gifts his heirs could reclaim.
A man sent specific new items to his father-in-law on Shavuot.

A man who suspected his betrothed had no sense of smell followed her into a ruin with a date to test her by making a false claim about a scent. A man tests his betrothed's sense of smell in a ruin, she correctly identifies a hidden date, but the ruin collapses on her, leading the Sages to rule he cannot inherit her property.
Issur the Convert, on his deathbed, successfully transfers a large sum of money held by Rava to his son Rav Mari by using a legal admission, despite Rava's attempts to find a way to keep the funds.
Rav Pappa transfers twelve thousand zuz located in Bei Huza'ei to Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa by granting him a small piece of land to facilitate the acquisition of the movable property.
The mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviyya transferred her property to her son to keep it from a future husband, but after being divorced, she sued to get it back.
A mother wrote two conflicting deeds to her two sons on consecutive days; after her death, the rabbis had to determine which son owned the property.
When the mother of Rav Amram the Pious died and left him promissory notes, his brothers challenged the gift because he hadn't physically seized them, but Rav Nahman upheld the gift.
A woman gave her property to one brother in the morning, but after her other brother came and cried to her in the evening, she changed her mind and gave it to him instead.
The sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef would repeatedly transfer her orchard to him whenever she fell ill, only to reclaim it upon recovery.
A sick woman directs that her expensive brooch be given to her daughter, and the Sages uphold the gift after her death despite it being only a partial gift of her property.
After Rav Naḥman responds to a legal question with a silent hand gesture and leaves, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asks Rava to interpret the meaning of that physical act.
A man who recovered from illness tries to retract a gift he made via a formal act of acquisition, but Rav Huna tells him he cannot.
A man seeks to retract a gift before Rav Nachman, who sends him to another rabbi so that the ruling can follow Rav's opinion without defying Shmuel's local authority.
The Gemara discusses a specific deed that lacked the standard formula regarding the giver's death.
An incident in Bnei Brak where a man sold his father's property and died, leading his family to contest the sale on the grounds that he was a minor.
In Bnei Brak, a man sold his father's inheritance and died, leading his family to challenge the sale's validity based on his age at the time of death.
A person sold his father's property during his transition year to adulthood, and Rava ruled the sale void.
A young man's sale was initially voided by Rava, but after the buyers coached him to challenge Rava on the price of legal documents, Rava realized the youth was savvy enough for the sale to be valid.
The mother of the sons of Rokhel, while sick, instructed that her expensive brooch be given to her daughter, and the Sages upheld her gift after her death.
A man from Meron in Jerusalem, wanting to distribute his movable property, bought a piece of land so he could legally link the gifts to the land transfer, a plan the Sages upheld after his death.
A man sells property named after 'bar Sisin' but later disputes a specific parcel with that name, leading Rav Nahman to rule in favor of the buyer and grant him possession.
A man challenges an occupant's right to a house, leading to a court case where Rav Nahman requires the occupant to prove his three-year residency.
Rami bar Hama cites an incident where a specific tied document was brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to challenge Rav Huna's definition of where witnesses sign.
A tied document is brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who misidentifies the date until Zunin explains the local dating custom, which the Rabbi then adopts.
It features a new actor (Rabbi Hanina) and a distinct legal case involving a different dating convention (Archon), though it follows the common 'case-and-ruling' pattern which can be borderline.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi nearly invalidates a tied document for lacking a date until his son Shimon suggests it is hidden in the folds, which is confirmed upon opening it.
While Shimon is reading Psalms, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi praises the scribe's handwriting, but when Shimon names the scribe, the Rabbi rebukes him for potentially inciting jealousy/gossip.
Ameimar validates a document based on one written and one oral witness, and dismisses Rav Ashi's objection based on Abaye's ruling.
After being expelled from the study hall, Rabbi Yirmeya provides such insightful answers to legal queries sent by his colleagues that he is brought back into the academy.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, distressed by the high price of sacrificial birds in Jerusalem, swears to lower the cost and immediately enters the court to change the law regarding women's obligations to bring offerings.
A dispute arises over a document stating a debt of 'six hundred and a dinar' without specifying the currency, leading Rav Sherevya to consult Abaye.
A tax collector asks Abaye for a signature sample to identify scholars, and Abaye provides it at the top of the page to prevent the collector from writing a debt above it.
A man forges a bill of sale by erasing parts of a letter to change 'in the orchard' to 'and the orchard,' but Abaye detects the forgery due to the unusual spacing.
A purchaser forges a document to include the portion of a brother named Aḥai by adding a 'vav', but Abaye catches him because the letters are too crowded.

Rava identifies his signature on a document but knows he never signed with the other witness, leading him to pressure the holder into confessing he found Rava's signature on a blank scrap and forged the note.
A woman claims she is not the one who signed a receipt witnessed by Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, and he confirms he does not recognize her.
A woman claims she is not the person named on a receipt signed by Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, but he identifies her as the correct person.

When landowners in Pumbedita were threatened by land-grabbing Arabs, they badgered Abaye into providing duplicate deeds, which he eventually did by instructing his scribe to write them in a technically invalid manner.
A woman sues her agent for buying land without a guarantee, and Rav Nachman orders the agent to purchase the land himself and resell it to her with the proper guarantee.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef sues Rabbi Abba for a debt before Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, who rules that Rabbi Abba must produce the witnesses he claims saw the repayment.
A baraita discusses the legal procedure for witnesses when a debtor repays half of a thousand-dinar debt.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef and Rabbi Abba bring a dispute over debt repayment to Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi, who rules that a receipt should be written despite his reverence for earlier authorities.
A promissory note with an anonymous creditor ('from you') is brought before Rav Huna's court, sparking a debate on its validity.
A judge allowed a creditor to seize property before a claim was made, but Rav Ḥanin son of Rav Yeiva intervened and physically expelled the creditor from the land.
A guarantor for a deceased man's debt paid the creditor without notifying the minor orphans and was subsequently denied reimbursement by the rabbis until the orphans reached majority.
A guarantor who repaid a gentile creditor before the orphans were claimed seeks reimbursement, leading to a legal debate between Rav Mordekhai and Rav Ashi.
Moshe bar Atzari guarantees his son's marriage contract, but a proposed legal maneuver involving divorce fails when it is discovered the son is a priest.
A case regarding a guarantor comes before Rabbi Yishmael, who is corrected by Ben Nannas, leading Rabbi Yishmael to praise the depth and wisdom of monetary law.
A case regarding a guarantor's liability is brought before Rabbi Yishmael, leading to a legal debate with Ben Nannas.
